newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - JAN 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - JAN 22.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The nine-day seamen's strike has led the government into a dangerous impasse with the unions. The government hopes to deal with the issue through judicial channels, with arrests in cases of violence or hindering transport. The strike has left more than 1,000 lorries stranded at Italian ports while farmers in Crete are in danger of losing their central European customers.

--The Central Archaeological Council admitted yesterday that recent finds in downtown Athens were "most probably" the famed Lyceum. The excavations will exist side-by-side with the Museum of Modern Art currently under construction at the site.
--Prime Minister Costas Simitis tells participants at the Socialist International in Rome yesterday that Turkey is a threat to peace in the region and wants to overturn the status quo in the Aegean.

--The government has prepared a package of measures - the carrot - and an action plan in case of protests - the stick - to avert the threats of new blockades by farmers. The conservative opposition, meanwhile, appears divided on its approach.
--The General Confederation of Workers of Greece (GSEE) yesterday appealed to deputies to vote down the government's new taxation bill, ahead of its 24-hour strike tomorrow.
--An impressive turnout for yesterday's march by striking teachers was the precursor to today's meeting between representatives and Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis.

--Development Minister Vasso Papandreou testified to the parliamentary fact-finding commission over revoking the licence for a casino in Athens. Papandreou laid the blame for the issue at the door of former tourism minister Dionysis Livanos, then responsible for the contract.
--Ionikos's Nigerian striker Amaechi Otitzi was released on bail after his arrest on charges of drug possession yesterday.
--The new real estate tax is so complicated that there are thoughts of sending tax officials to special seminars while taxpayers will have to resort to accountants.
--The Greek islands are facing enormous problems due to the 10-day seamen's strike, with lorries immobilised on docks.
--A Turkish drug dealer is considered to be a key to resolving the dramatic kidnapping of a nightclub owner on Saturday night.
--The government's continuing intransigence is pushing things to the limits, ND leader Miltiades Evert claimed yesterday. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
